To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cluster size in Cu+Cu and central Au+Au is similar to that in p+p collisions, but that there is an increase of the cluster size as a function of centrality, and the cluster size in semi-central Cu and Au collisions scales with the number of participant nucleons.
the two-particle angular correlation function in heavy ion collisions is a complex function that can be described by a cluster model.

we observe that the size of the clusters of particles created in heavy ion and p+p collisions scales with the fraction of total cross-section, which is proportional to the impact parameter divided by the radius of the nucleus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of particle production in high energy collisions, in particular in the heavy ion collisions at RHIC.
the understanding of the space-time evolution of the medium created in high energy heavy ion collisions, and the hadronization process in such collisions.
the study of particle production in high energy collisions of protons, copper and gold ions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cluster size is a sensitive probe for the system size, but it does not seem to be sensitive to the system temperature.
the cluster size in semi-central heavy ion collisions is comparable to p+p, but increases with decreasing centrality.
the two-particle correlation function shows that the cluster size increases with centrality in both p+p and A+A collisions and is independent of the system size in central collisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found that the two-particle correlations in heavy ion collisions have a strong geometric dependence.
the system size dependence of the correlation structure is not consistent with a simple picture of a single particle source.
the cluster model is a good description of the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the size of the cluster is not a function of centrality but a function of the number of participating nucleons.
the cluster size in semi-central Cu-Cu and Au-Au collisions is comparable to the one observed in p-p collisions.
the size of clusters in semi-central heavy ion collisions is comparable to the size of clusters formed in p+p collisions.
